newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - E. EUROPE NOT READY YET FOR MUNI BOND BOOM.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - E. EUROPE NOT READY YET FOR MUNI BOND BOOM.

text.p: More East European cities are eyeing trendy municipal bond issues but low liquidity and closed tenders are likely to keep the potentially dynamic market from booming for a while.

Municipal bonds, which offer cash-hungry cities cheap credit while yielding high returns for investors, are likely to be available only to a select few buyers until secondary markets develop throughout the former communist states.

Analysts say that a region-wide boom was probably still at least a year away because most countries have to catch up with frontrunners, the Czech Republic and Slovenia, which already have municipal bonds on secondary securities markets.

"There was a tremendous pick-up in muni bond issues in 1996, but there are limitations as many offers are not public and are limited by small volume," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist of WoodCommerz in Warsaw.
Despite these shortcomings, municipal bond launches across the former East bloc have met with success as yields at 100 to 300 basis points above comparable treasuries drew investors.

Investors said municipal bond issues done through credible financial advisers were not much more risky than local currency government debt because, in many countries, municipal incomes were based on state-distributed funds.

The Czech Republic has been the region's leader in developing a secondary market for municipal bonds. So far nine cities have issued bonds worth 2.7 billion crowns ($100 million) but daily turnover remains low at around $1 million.

Analysts said that even the region's most developed market had not reached its potential, partially because Czechs have traditionally been debt avoiders and also because many towns were so small that they deemed an issue too costly.

However, 12 municipalities in northern and central Moravia were about to take a new approach. They were thinking of banding together for a single, one billion crown issue, which if successful could be one of several such offers.

Prague, the first municipal borrower in Eastern Europe to make use of Eurobonds with a $250 million issue in 1994, was also rumoured to be looking at the yen and deutschemark sectors for its next visit to international markets, analysts said.
The outlook for the Czech muni bond sector is fairly positive and trading volume is expected to pick up slowly as municipalites catch on, analysts said.

Slovenian muni bonds, accounting for about three percent of the capitalisation of the Ljubljana Stock Exchange, have not been attractive as most are denominated in marks which weakened in real terms against the Slovenian tolar last year.
Central Europe's other municipal bond markets are in various stages of development, with Poland's the most advanced of the rest and likely to bloom at the turn of this year.
So far most Polish municipal issues have been small, private placements while secondary trade is virtually non-existent, but analysts expect the market to expand gradually as more cities join in.

"This year could be the year for municipal debt in Poland as issuers begin to realise their plans after observing initial offers in 1996," said Arkadiusz Bubak, adviser at the Capital Operations Centre of Bank Handlowy SA.

Polish pioneer Ostrow Wielkopolski, which late last year cleared its 7.5 million zloty ($2.6 million) muni bond issue for public trade, was likely to become the country's first city listed on the developing over-the-counter market (CTO).

"A CTO listing, expected roughly at the end of the first quarter, will give our town great marketing and increase the liquidity of our bonds, which is good news for investors," said Jolanta Szeprzynska, spokeswoman for Ostrow in western Poland.
"Other municipalites are watching us and may follow suit if our CTO launch is a success," Szeprzynska added.

Analysts said Gdansk's 99 million zloty issue expected in the first quarter of this year, by far the largest Polish muni bond issue, could be a signpost for future launches and a potential pillar for the development of secondary markets.

They said Hungary, with no municipal bond launches since 1993, was unlikely to regain the initiative this year, although a new securities law offered better conditions for muni bond issues and opened the gate for renewed interest.

Analysts said the development of Hungary's municipals was hindered by the dominance on its securities market of bank-controlled brokerages, which were more interested in lending to cities than in managing issues for them.

Romania, where the municipal bond market is also in its infancy, has three cities -- the capital Bucharest, the Black Sea port of Constanta and the mountain resort of Brasov -- which have shown interest in internatinal issues.
Bucharest's city hall said it planned to raise $200 million through Merrill Lynch, while Constanta and Brasov plan to raise up to $150 million each through Salomon Brothers. REUTER
